title: Londonderry Air
origin: Irish air from County Londonderry, noted from Jane Ross of Limavady and first printed by George Petrie in 1855

pd.detail: First published in George Petrie, 'The Ancient Music of Ireland' (Dublin, 1855), from a manuscript supplied by Jane Ross of Limavady, County Londonderry; the air itself is older and anonymous.
pd.sourceEdition: Petrie, George, 'The Ancient Music of Ireland' vol. 1 (Dublin, 1855), the untitled air from County Londonderry; encoded transposed to C major as a single melodic line.
pd.notes: The 1913 'Danny Boy' text by Frederic Edward Weatherly IS carried, on its own separate basis: Weatherly died in 1929, more than 95 years ago, so the words clear on the lyricist's dates independently of the anonymous air (see each section's lyrics.pd, which uses author-died-pre-1930 rather than published-pre-1930 because the 1913 first printing was London, not the US). Only Weatherly's first verse is carried; his second verse is not, and no other text set to this air is. No 20th-century arrangement is carried; this is the traditional air reduced to its tune with plain diatonic changes.

notes: Common time throughout, a slow air. 32 bars encoded as four 8-bar sections (A, A', B, A''), each section carrying two sung lines of four bars. The single-note anacrusis that opens the air lives in the last beat of the intro; every later line's pickup sits at the end of the preceding section.

pd.detail: Frederic Edward Weatherly (1848-1929) wrote these words in 1910 and reset them to the Londonderry Air in 1913. He died in September 1929, more than 95 years ago, which clears the WORDS worldwide on the lyricist's own dates and does not depend on where the song was first printed. The 1913 first publication was Boosey, London, so the published-pre-1930 basis (which the SPEC defines as US first publication) is NOT the ground relied on here; the term expired in the US in any case, 95 years from 1913 publication.
pd.sourceEdition: Weatherly's 'Danny Boy' as published by Boosey, 1913; read from the public-domain text of that first printing, not from any later recorded performance or arrangement.

lyrics.notes: Weatherly's first verse, two lines per section across the four sung sections. One stanza each: the form plays every section exactly once, so no occurrence needs a second set of words. Every line of this air begins on a single-beat anacrusis and lands its stressed syllable on the following downbeat, so lines are pinned to that downbeat bar: line 1 to bar 0 (its pickup 'Oh' is the last beat of the intro) and line 2 to bar 4 (its pickup 'From' is the note at beat 15, the last beat of bar 3). Line 1's eleven syllables run pickup plus bars 0-3; line 2's ten run pickup plus bars 4-7.

stanzas.text: Oh, Danny Boy, the pipes, the pipes are calling
From glen to glen, and down the mountain side,

lyrics.notes: Lines 3 and 4 of the verse. Line 3's pickup ('The') sits on the last beat of the preceding section, so the line is pinned to bar 0 here; line 4's pickup ('It's') is the note at beat 15, so it is pinned to the downbeat of bar 4.

stanzas.text: The summer's gone, and all the roses falling,
It's you, it's you must go and I must bide.

lyrics.notes: Lines 5 and 6, the turn of the verse. This is the section that leaps to the high tonic, and the word stress lands on that leap at bar 0 ('come'), its pickup 'But' being the last beat of the preceding section. Line 6's pickup ('Or') is the note at beat 15, so the line is pinned to the downbeat of bar 4.

stanzas.text: But come ye back when summer's in the meadow,
Or when the valley's hushed and white with snow,

lyrics.notes: The closing couplet, lines 7 and 8, over the final statement of the head. Line 8's twelve syllables match the twelve notes from the beat-15 pickup through the final long tonic at beat 28, so the line is pinned to the downbeat of bar 4.

stanzas.text: It's I'll be here in sunshine or in shadow,
Oh, Danny Boy, oh Danny Boy, I love you so!
